content: Male circumcision for adolescent boys and men in areas with generalized HIV epidemics has been associated with satisfaction and a belief in enhanced sexual performance. However, there is no scientific evidence to support the claim that voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) improves sexual performance, and this should not be used as a reason to promote circumcision. Barriers to the uptake of VMMC include fear or uncertainty about pain, injury, complications, and adverse events; negative perceptions influenced by religious or cultural beliefs; loss of wages due to time off work; the requirement for sexual abstinence during the healing period; feelings of shame; and the perception that the benefits of the procedure are not relevant. The World Health Organization (WHO) conducted a scoping review of peer-reviewed literature to identify evidence-based interventions aimed at increasing the uptake of VMMC among adult men. This was followed by systematic reviews of interventions with more than three comparative studies. The findings highlighted that no specific recommendations were made regarding service delivery interventions or economic compensation due to limited evidence and the diversity of intervention types. The quality of evidence was moderate to high for service delivery interventions and low to moderate for economic compensation. Service delivery interventions addressed barriers related to access, awareness, self-efficacy, and acceptability. Changes to the way VMMC services were delivered, such as community-based, facility-based, and school-based approaches, were found to enhance uptake. These interventions were implemented in diverse settings, including health facilities, communities, homes, and schools. Countries and implementers are encouraged to consider approaches that best suit their populations and contexts. Community-based approaches included intensified campaigns at fixed sites, community outreach at primary health facilities, workplaces, and schools, and services provided at local dispensaries or non-healthcare facilities in underserved areas identified using geographic information systems (GIS). Home-based services linked to facilities, HIV testing, and broader HIV and VMMC education using referral and reminder approaches, such as text messages or home visits, were also employed. Facility-based approaches included offering HIV testing and linking to VMMC services, training healthcare workers to improve service delivery, engaging female partners and mothers of adolescent boys, and improving service quality at outreach sites by enhancing privacy and involving female partners. Schooland sports-based approaches targeted adolescents and included components such as mentorship programs, football-based coaching interventions, in-school education, and client-friendly appointment times. These interventions often involved transportation to service sites and peer recruitment. Economic compensation was studied as a means to enhance VMMC uptake among adolescents and adults. Compensation included fixed amounts, prizes in lotteries, food, transportation, or subsidized vouchers for circumcision at health facilities. Fixed compensation, particularly to cover transportation or opportunity costs, was associated with higher uptake among adult men. However, lottery-based approaches and variable compensation amounts did not lead to greater uptake. The WHO Guideline Development Group decided against recommending economic compensation due to concerns about feasibility, ethics, acceptability, and human rights. Evidence on compensation was limited, particularly for adolescents. Decisions regarding the use, type, and amount of compensation require community engagement, input from local stakeholders, and consideration of the specific context and broader health system, including its impact on universal health coverage. Economic compensation may address access barriers by reducing costs, such as transportation and lost wages, and was generally considered acceptable by clients. However, some community leaders expressed reservations about compensation. Service delivery interventions were defined as changes to the ways in which VMMC services are delivered. These included improved training of healthcare workers, restructuring physical spaces and site organization, providing services at different hours or locations, and offering additional health education during or after VMMC. Nearly all service delivery interventions were associated with improved VMMC uptake, with randomized controlled trials providing high to moderate quality evidence and observational studies providing low-quality evidence. People-centered health care, which adopts the perspectives of individuals, families, and communities as participants in and beneficiaries of trusted health systems, was emphasized. This approach focuses on the comprehensive needs of people rather than individual diseases and respects social preferences. It also requires that patients have the education and support needed to make decisions and participate in their care, while caregivers work in supportive environments. In summary, service delivery interventions, particularly those that are people-centered and address barriers to access and acceptability, may enhance the uptake of VMMC. However, the evidence remains limited, and interventions should be tailored to the specific needs and contexts of the target populations.
